Perform
per-form'
v. (to carry through to completion; to fulfil what was promised or vowed; rendering Hebrew asah and qum, Greek epiteleo and poieo)
From Old French parfournir, to complete or furnish through, from par (thoroughly) and fournir, to furnish. The buried sense is not display but completion — to perform a thing is to carry it all the way out.

Biblical Definition

To perform in Scripture is to bring a word to its accomplishment, and the doctrine turns on who is doing it. Of God it is stated as a settled character: he is watching over his own speech, “for I will hasten my word to perform it” (Jeremiah 1:12) — spoken to a young prophet who had just objected that he was a child, and given in the form of a pun on the almond tree, the watching-tree that wakes first in the year. Abraham's faith is defined by the same verb: he was “fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform” (Romans 4:21). Faith, in Paul's definition, is confidence in a promiser's competence, not optimism about outcomes. The best-known instance is Paul's confidence for a church: “he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6) — the beginning and the completing are both God's, which is the doctrine of perseverance stated as a pastoral certainty. Of man the verb appears as vow-keeping, and it costs: “I have sworn, and I will perform it, that I will keep thy righteous judgments” (Psalm 119:106). To swear is easy and to perform is the whole of the matter, which is why Ecclesiastes warns that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.

Webster 1828 Definition

To carry through to completion. God hastens his word to perform it and completes the work he began; faith is being persuaded he is able to perform; and a man's vow is nothing until performed.

expand to see more

PERFORM, v.t. [L. per and formo, or Fr. parfournir, to complete.] To do; to execute; to accomplish; to carry through to the end.

2. To execute; to discharge; as, to perform a duty or a promise.

3. To fulfil; as, to perform a covenant or a vow.

4. PERFORM, v.i. To do; to act a part; as, the actor performed well.

5. PERFORMANCE, n. Execution or completion of any thing; a deed or action done.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 1:12 — "Then said the LORD unto me, Thou hast well seen: for I will hasten my word to perform it."

Romans 4:21 — "And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform."

Philippians 1:6 — "Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:"

Psalm 119:106 — "I have sworn, and I will perform it, that I will keep thy righteous judgments."

Modern Corruption

Philippians 1:6 is applied as a general reassurance about a man's plans, when it is a promise about God's work of salvation — and vows are made lightly because performing them is no longer thought to matter.

expand to see more

Philippians 1:6 is one of the most misapplied verses in common use, pressed into service to assure people that whatever project or ambition God has supposedly begun in them will succeed. Paul is speaking of a good work in a specific sense: the salvation of the Philippians, begun when the gospel came to them by a riverside and a jailer's house, and completed at the day of Jesus Christ. That is why the verse is a comfort. It rests the believer's perseverance on God's completion rather than on his own consistency, and it is the ordinary Reformed doctrine that those whom God effectually calls he also keeps. Applied to careers and plans it becomes a promise God never made and experience will break.

The principle to recover is the seriousness of performing what is vowed. Psalm 119:106 is a man binding himself with an oath to keep God's judgments, and Scripture treats such words as debts. When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools (Ecclesiastes 5:4). Membership promises, marriage vows, and ordination pledges are made in an age that has largely stopped believing words create obligations, and the wreckage is visible. The remedy is not fewer vows but performed ones, and the model is God himself, who watches over his word to do it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew asah is to do or make; qum, to raise up, is used of performing a word or oath. Greek epiteleo is to complete; poieo, to do.

expand to see more

Hebrew asah (H6213) — to do, make, accomplish; the common verb of performing a thing.

Hebrew qum (H6965) — to raise up, to make good; used of performing an oath or word.

Hebrew shaqad (H8245) — to watch, to hasten; the pun on the almond tree in Jeremiah 1:11-12.

Greek epiteleo (G2005) — to complete, to finish; will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.

Greek poieo (G4160) — to do, to make; the general verb of doing what was said.

Usage

"Of God watching over his own word: I will hasten my word to perform it (Jeremiah 1:12)."

"Of faith defined: what he had promised, he was able also to perform (Romans 4:21)."

"Of a vow made and to be kept: I have sworn, and I will perform it (Psalm 119:106)."
